sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
While electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) is a highly desirable approach for converting CO2 into highly-valued fuels and chemicals, the design and create of efficient CO2RR catalysts with excellent selectivity to desirable product and long-term stability still remains great challenge. In this work, we have successfully created a series of bimetallic CuSn nanowires (NWs) with modulated phases and structures as superior electrocatalysts for CO2RR. Three distinct CuSn NWs, namely, CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, have been created by the combination of hydrothermal process and controlled thermal treatment in different atmospheres, where the optimized CuSn NWs/C-Air shows significant enhanced activity with the best formate selectivity of 90.2% at -1.0 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode under alkaline condition, which is much higher than those of CuSn NWs/C-H2 (62.6%) and CuSn NWs/C-N2 (64.3%). Moreover, the unique CuSn NWs/C-Air also exhibits enhanced stability without significant activity and selectivity degradation after continuous operating about 10 h. Density functional theory calculations reveal that Sn atoms doping into CuO(111) surface, enhancing the adsorption of CO2 intermediate *OCHO and suppressing H2 production, could be the plausible site to realize the high selective CO2RR observed in CuSn NWs/C-Air. The realization of one-dimensional (1D) heterostructures with precisely modulated phases and structures hold significant promise for the design of efficient electrocatalysts and beyond.
Graphical Abstract
Keywords: nanowire, carbon dioxide reduction reaction, electrocatalysis, CuSn, modulated phase and structure

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2), a greenhouse gas that increases as a result of fossil fuels burning, has caused series of environment problems such as global warming, seawater acidification and sea level rise.[1-4] The conversion of CO2 into highly-valued fuels and chemicals, like formate (HCOOH) and carbon monoxide (CO), is a promising strategy for achieving the goal of simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas and utilizing carbon resources in CO2.[5-8] Among various CO2 conversion strategies, electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is attracting extensive attention owing to their mild operating conditions and achievable conversion efficiencies, however, the high energy barriers and proton coupling multi-electron steps result in a major challenge for yielding desirable products. Cubased materials are considered as potential electrocatalysts for CO2RR due to their potential products of HCOOH, CO, methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4) and even other hydrocarbons.[9-11] Although tremendous efforts have been made, it is regrettable that the selectivity, namely Faradaic efficiency (FE), and stability of theses catalysts are still far from satisfactory.
To date, the main research focus is on the relationship between composition, shape, size and
electrochemical performance, but the effects of phase and structure are limited.[12-15] In fact, several
studies have demonstrated that the catalytic activity depends not only on composition, shape and size, but also on phase and structure, especially for oxygen evolution reaction and hydrogen evolution reaction.[16-18] Yu and co-workers have selectively synthesized hierarchical CoTe2 and CoTe nanofleeces by changing the amount of Co precursors and increasing the reaction temperature, in which CoTe2 shows enhanced OER activity and stability under alkaline environment.[19] Our group have reported platinum-nickel nanowires (Pt-Ni NWs) with controlled interfaces and phases as efficient HER electrocatalysts under universal conditions, where the optimized Pt-Ni NWs/C-Air exhibits superior electroctalytic performance due to their unique one-dimensional (1D) nanostructures with controlled interfaces and phases.[20] In fact, NWs are ideal 1D nanostructures owing to their inherent anisotropy, high flexibility and advanced ability to modulate phases and structures along the longitudinal direction of NWs.[21-25] The phase and structure controlled NWs are particularly fascinating because they can potentially modulate the electronic properties to tune the binding strength of adsorbate, being expected to create highly efficient CO2RR electrocatalysts. Nevertheless, the delicate control of 1D NWs with modulated phases and structures for efficient CO2RR has largely unexplored, which could be a promising strategy to design high-performance CO2RR electrocatalysts.
Herein, we developed a series of bimetallic CuSn NWs with modulated phases and structures as
superior electrocatalysts for CO2RR. Three distinct CuSn NWs with different phases and structures, namely, CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2 by heating treatment at 300 °C for 1h in air, 5% hydrogen (H2)/95% nitrogen (N2) mixed gas and N2, respectively, have been successfully created. Significantly, the optimized CuSn NWs/C-Air exhibits boosted electrochemical CO2RR activity with FEHCOOH of 90.2% at -1.0 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (vs. RHE), which outperform than those of CuSn NWs/C-H2 (62.6%) and CuSn NWs/C-N2 (64.3%), respectively. The CuSn NWs/CAir is also very stable with negligible degradation even after continuous operation for up to 10 h.
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that Sn atoms doping into CuO(111) surface, enhancing the adsorption of CO2 intermediate * OCHO and suppressing H2 production, could be the plausible site to realize the high selective CO2RR observed in CuSn NWs/C-Air.

sections.heading: Chemicals
sections.text: Copper (II) chloride dihydrate (CuCl2·2H2O, AR), glucose (C6H12O6·H2O, 98%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, AR) and isopropanol (IPA, AR) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. Tin (II) acetate (SnAC2·4H2O, 95%) was obtained from Alfa Aesar. Oleylamine (CH3(CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CH2NH2, 70%) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Nitrogen (N2, 99.999%) and carbon dioxide (CO2, 99.999%) were purchased from WuGang Gas Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

sections.heading: Preparations of Cu NWs and CuSn NWs
sections.text: First, 13.6 mg CuCl2·2H2O, 4.7 mg SnAC2·4H2O, 15.8 mg glucose were dissolved into 5 mL H2O. Then, 160 μL oleylamine and 3 mL H2O were added into above solution. The mixture was transferred to a 30 mL Teflon-sealed autoclave after sonication about 30 min and maintained at 120 °C about 12 h. The products were collected by centrifugation and washed with cyclohexane/ethanol mixture. The preparation of Cu NWs was similar to that of CuSn NWs but without adding SnAC2·4H2O.

sections.heading: Preparations of Cu NWs/C, CuSn NWs/C, CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2
sections.text:
CuSn NWs were deposited on Vulcan XC72R carbon (30wt%, determined by ICP-AES) by sonicated for 30 min in 10 mL cyclohexane. The products were washed server times with cyclohexane/ethanol. The obtained CuSn NWs/C was dried at 60 °C in an oven and then annealed at 300 °C for 1 h in air, 5% hydrogen (H2)/95% nitrogen (N2) mixed gas and N2, respectively. The final products were denoted as
CuSn NWs/C, CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, respectively. The preparation of Cu NWs/C was similar to the preparation of CuSn NWs/C, and the final product was denoted as Cu NWs/C.

sections.heading: Characterization
sections.text: Low-magnification transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was conducted on a HITACHI HT7700 transmission electron microscope with acceleration voltage of 120 kV. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM-EDS) element mappings were conducted on a FEI Tecnai F20 transmission electron microscope with acceleration voltage of 200 kV. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns were collected on X’Pert-Pro MPD diffractometer (Netherlands PANalytical) with a Cu Kα X-ray source (λ = 1.540598 Å). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was done with an SSI S-Probe XPS Spectrometer. The carbon peak at 284.6 eV was used as a reference to correct for charging effects.

sections.heading: Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
A CHI660 electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai) with three-electrode cell was used to measure CO2RR performance. A carbon paper (Toray, 1 cm × 1 cm), micro Ag/AgCl electrode and graphite rod were used as working, reference and counter electrode, respectively. The ink was obtained by ultrasonicating the mixture with 400 µL IPA, 200 µL H2O and 5 µL 5 wt% Nafion and 6mg catalysts. 300 µL suspension was deposited on carbon paper and then dried at 80 °C.
Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction was performed on a CHI660 (Chenhua, Shanghai)
electrochemical workstation with a typical H-type cell and separated by Nafion 117 anion exchange membrane. The gas chromatograph (GC Agilent 7890B) was connected with the cathodic compartment to monitor gas phase compositions. Liquid products were characterized by 1 H NMR on Agilent 600MHz
DirectDrive2 spectrometers. The faradaic efficiency (FE) for the formation of hydrocarbon was calculated as follows: FE = eF × n/Q = 2F × n/(I × t), where e is the number of electrons transferred, F is the Faraday constant, Q is the charge, I is the current, t is the running time and n is the total amount of product (in mole).

sections.heading: Computational details
sections.text: Spin-polarized first-principles calculations were realized by the software Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP).[26] In order to get accurate adsorption energy and thermodynamics, the description of exchange-correction functional adopted the generalized gradient approximation of the revised-PerdewBurke-Ernzerhof (GGA-RPBE) formula in a plane wave pseudopotential implementation.[27] The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV and the thresholds of total energy and force during geometry optimization were 10 -4 eV and 0.05 eV/Å. Then the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model was used to evaluate the transfer proton and electron in which the chemical potential of the proton-electron pair was equal to half of the chemical potential of gases hydrogen molecule.[28] Then the applied electrode potential was considered by ∆G=-eU, where e is the elementary positive charge and U is the applied potential.

sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
The CuSn NWs with core-shell structure were initially obtained by an efficient hydrothermal approach, in which copper (II) chloride dihydrate (CuCl2·2H2O) and tin (II) acetate (SnAc2·4H2O) were metal precursors and water (H2O) was solvent. The morphology of CuSn NWs was performed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). It is obvious that the product consists of 1D nanostructure with high uniformity (Figure 1a). Interestingly, there is an amorphous shell surround the surface of NWs, as revealed by the enlarged TEM image (Figure 1b). The diameter of CuSn NWs was measured to be 21.8
± 2.9 nm, larger than that of Cu NWs (17.1 ± 2.7 nm) (Figure S1-2). The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image reveal that the clear lattice spacing of 0.209 nm was belong to the (111) plane of Cu and the amorphous shell with thickness of around 2.0 nm were observed (Figure 1c). The overall Cu/Sn composition was about 4:1 and determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES) and scanning electron microscopy energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) (Figure 1d). Power X-ray diffraction (PXRD) was used to analyze the phase change and structure evolution (Figure 1e), where the positions of main diffraction peaks were located at 43.3 o , 50.4 o and 74.1 o , corresponding to the (111), (200) and (220) planes of metallic Cu (PDF#04-0836), respectively. No significant diffraction peaks for Sn species can be observed, further proving that Sn species in CuSn NWs is amorphous. The valence state and electron structure of Sn species were measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), two peaks with the binding energies (BEs) of 495.2 eV (3d3/2) and 486.9 eV (3d5/2) can be assigned to Sn 4+ , respectively, showing that the amorphous Sn species in CuSn NWs is of SnO2 (Figure 1f).[29,30] The elemental distribution of CuSn NWs was confirmed by scanning TEM-EDS (STEM-EDS) element mappings (Figure 1g), where Sn is rich surround the NWs and Cu is limited in the inner region, demonstrating that the CuSn NWs have core-shell structures.
Fig 1. (a, b) TEM images and atom model, (c) HRTEM image, (d) SEM-EDS spectrum, (e) XRD pattern, (f) Sn 3d XPS spectrum and (g) STEM-EDS element mappings of CuSn NWs. Red, green and gray balls represent the oxygen, copper and tin atoms.
A series of bimetallic CuSn NWs with modulated phases and structures were constructed by
controlling the thermal annealing treatments in different atmospheres, including air, 5% hydrogen (H2)/95% nitrogen (N2) mixed gas and N2. The phases and structures of CuSn NWs after thermal
treatment in different atmospheres were also investigated by XRD, TEM, and STEM-EDS element mappings. The PXRD pattern of CuSn NWs/C-Air shows that the main peaks of metallic Cu vanish and two new sharp diffraction peaks appear at about 35.6 o and 38.8 o (Figure 2a), matching well with the (- 111) and (111) planes of CuO (PDF#80-1268), respectively. In addition, a weak broad peak located at about 26.6 o , which can be assigned to the (110) plane of SnO2, was observed. The phase changes of CuSn NWs/C-Air prove that the metallic Cu was oxidized and the crystallinity of SnO2 was generated after heating the pristine CuSn NWs in air at 300 °C for 1 h. For CuSn NWs/C-H2, the main peaks of metallic Cu still maintain without new peak appears, showing that no obvious phase change occurred under H2 atmosphere. In addition, while the PXRD pattern of CuSn NWs/C-N2 shows similar diffraction peaks of metallic Cu as those of CuSn NWs/C, four new weak peaks can be observed at 26.6 o , 33.9 o , 38.0 o and 51.8 o , belonging to the (110), (101), (200) and (211) planes of SnO2 (PDF#77-0447), respectively.
The morphologies and structures of CuSn NWs after thermal treatment in different atmospheres
have been also investigated. TEM images show that the pristine CuSn NWs have changed into rugged structure with slightly increasing the diameter to 29.2 ± 2.7 nm after annealing in air at 300 °C for 1h (Figure 2b&Figure S3a-c). The HRTEM image of CuSn NWs/C-Air reveals the lattice spacing is 0.232 nm, corresponding to the (111) plane of CuO (Figure 2c). Another lattice spacing of 0.335 nm can be found, in consistent with the (110) plane of SnO2. Composition distribution of CuSn NWs/C-Air was analyzed by STEM-EDS element mappings (Figure 2d), where the Cu and Sn were evenly distributed on the NWs. These significantly changes in crystalline structure and morphology of CuSn NWs/C-Air demonstrate that the interior metallic Cu gradually diffused outside and transformed into CuO after postannealing treatment under air, accompanying with increased size and formation of rugged structure. For CuSn NWs/C-H2, the NW structures were largely maintained with an average diameter of 23.4 ± 2.7 nm,
while a large number of nanoparticles (NPs) appeared on the surface of NWs (Figure 2e&Figure S4ac). The HRTEM image of CuSn NWs/C-H2 is shown in Figure 2f, where the 0.209 nm interplanar spacing correspond to the (111) plane of metallic Cu, while amorphous SnO2 can also be observed in red dashed lines. In order to investigate the composition of CuSn NWs/C-H2, STEM-EDS element mappings were performed (Figure 2g). It can be seen that the CuSn NWs/C-H2 exhibits 1D heterostructure with NPs comprised of Cu and Sn species on the surface of NWs, demonstrating that the interior Cu gradually diffused outside to form NPs, and the amorphous SnO2 also migrated to form NPs under H2 atmosphere at 300 °C. In contrast, while the CuSn NWs/C-N2 without obvious changes at first glance, the enlarged TEM image shows that the shell became rough (Figure 2h&Figure S5a-c). The major lattice fringes with the average spacing of CuSn NWs/C-N2 are 0.335 nm and 0.209 nm, which can be assigned to the (110) plane of SnO2 and the (111) plane of metallic Cu, respectively (Figure 2i). STEM-EDS element mappings also confirm that the NWs consist of Cu core as central axis and Sn species adhere on its surface as shell. The Cu/Sn atomic ratio of CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2 are about 4:1 and determined by ICP-AES and SEM-EDS analysis (Figures S3d&S4d&S5d), showing that the thermal treatment in different atmospheres do hardly cause composition changes.
Fig 2. (a) PXRD patterns and corresponding atom models of CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2. (b) TEM image, (c) HRTEM image and (d) STEM-EDS element mappings of CuSn NWs/C-Air. (e) TEM image, (f) HRTEM image and (g) STEM-EDS element mappings of CuSn NWs/C-H2. (h) TEM image, (i) HRTEM image and (j) STEM-EDS element mappings of CuSn NWs/C-N2. # in (a) represents C peak. Red, green and gray balls represent the oxygen, copper and tin atoms.
In order to explore the effects of phase and structure on electrocatalysis, various catalysts were
thoroughly investigated for electrochemical CO2RR in 0.5 M KHCO3 under ambient conditions. The CO2RR performances of these catalysts were performed by chronoamperometry method under different
potentials (Figure S6). The gaseous and liquid products were analyzed by gas chromatography and nuclear magnetic resonance, respectively (Figures S7&S8). Linear sweeping voltammetry method was carried out to obtain the polarization curves of various catalysts by using a typical H-type cell with standard three-electrode system (Figure 3a). Compared with Cu NWs/C, the pristine CuSn NWs/C exhibits lower current density under the same conditions, which may be attributed to the presence of amorphous SnO2 shell on the surface. Significantly, all CuSn NWs after thermal treatment in different atmospheres show enhanced current density, suggesting that the changes of phases and structures result in enhanced current response. To support the above hypothesis, FEs of major products for these catalysts as a function of different cathode potentials are shown in Figure 3b-f. It is found that the main product of Cu NWs/C is H2 in the potential range from -0.7 V to -1.2 V vs. RHE, and a small amount of CO, HCOOCH, ethylene (C2H4) and ethane (C2H6) could also be detected (Figure 3b&Figure S9). For CuSn NWs/C, the FE of H2 reduced significantly while HCOOH increased dramatically, proving that the amorphous SnO2 on the surfaces of Cu NWs can promote the conversion efficiency of CO2 into HCOOH and depress the H2 production. Compared with CuSn NWs/C, CuSn NWs/C-Air exhibits higher FE for HCOOH and lower FE for H2, revealing that the thermal treatment under air can further improve the HCOOH selectivity of CO2RR. The CuSn NWs/C-H2 reveals a slightly higher FEHCOOH than that of FECO at low applied voltage, while the FEH2 gradually exceeds that of FEHCOOH with the increase of applied voltage. For CuSn NWs/C-N2, the HCOOH and H2 maintained the similar FE values with the highest FEHCOOH at -1.0 V vs. RHE. Importantly, the highest FEHCOOH of CuSn NWs/C-Air reaches 90.2% at -1.0 V vs. RHE, which is significantly higher than those of CuSn NWs/C-N2 (64.3%), CuSn NWs/C-H2 (62.6%), CuSn NWs/C (59.9%) and Cu NWs/C (17.6%), respectively. Such excellent HCOOH selectivity surpasses most reported CO2RR electrocatalysts (Table S1). Moreover, the HCOOH, H2 and CO partial current densities of different catalysts are shown in Figure S10, where the
HCOOH partial current density of CuSn NWs/C-Air achieves -17.33 mA cm -2 at -1.0 V vs. RHE, which is 1.4, 1.5, 2.3 and 4.2 times than those of CuSn NWs/C-N2 (-12.53 mA cm -2 ), CuSn NWs/C-H2 (-11.72 mA cm -2 ), CuSn NWs/C (-7.45 mA cm -2 ) and Cu NWs/C (-4.15 mA cm -2 ), respectively. Additionally, CuSn NWs/C-Air with different atomic ratios were also prepared as references (Figure S11,12). To investigate the intrinsic activity of controlled CuSn NWs, electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was performed (Figure S13 and Table S2). It is worth noting that, for CuSn NWs/C-Air improved ECSA was observed for enhanced CO2RR. To further evaluate the kinetic and mechanism pathway for the formation of HCOOH, the Tafel slope of controlled CuSn NWs and possible schematic mechanism were carried out (Figure S14). Compared with CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, the lower Tafel slope for HCOOH can be observed in CuSn NWs/C-Air, indicating the faster reaction kinetics. As displayed, After the formation of CO2 * from the dissolved CO2, the CO2 * is then adsorbed on the surface of CuSn NWs. Subsequently, the adsorbed CO2* will reduced by an electron to obtain CuSn NWsCO2* - intermediate. This intermediate readily forms adsorbed HCOO* - by combining with H + and e - , resulting in the formation of HCOOH. For CuSn NWs/C-Air, the Tafel slope for HCOOH of 58 mV dec - 1 , indicating that the rate-determining steps (RDS) of CO2 electroreduction to form HCOOH on the CuSn NW/C-Air is the protonation process of CO2* - . However, the Tafel slope show a higher value of 80 mV dec -1 and 65 mV dec -1
for CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, respectively, demonstrating
that the formation of CO2* - intermediate is the RDS step. Finally, the stability of CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2 were evaluated by using the chronoamperometry at -1.0 V vs. RHE (Figure S15). Noticeably, all catalysts maintained stable current density after continuous operating for 10 h with the constant FE values for HCOOH, H2 and CO. The morphology and composition were also investigated after electrocatalysis, as shown in Figure S16, the CuSn NWs/C-Air still maintained the 1D NWs structure with only slight change in the overall atomic ratio of Cu/Sn. In addition, the
PXRD pattern reveals that the SnO2 species maintained well, while CuO was reduced to Cu2O and Cu during the CO2RR process (Figure S17a). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis further demonstrates the Cu 2+ was reduced to Cu + and Cu 0 after electrocatalysis while there was no significant change for Sn species (Figure S17b-d), confirming that the tin oxide could be a stable active site to activate CO2.
In view the interesting phenomenon between phase, structure and electrochemical CO2RR
performance, the chemical states and electronic properties of various NWs were investigated (Figure 4). It can be seen that the Cu 2p XPS peaks of Cu NWs/C are located at 951.3 eV and 931.5 eV, corresponding to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 of Cu 0, + (Figure 4a).[31-33] However, the Cu 2p XPS peaks of CuSn NWs/C shift to 951.5 eV and 931.8 eV after the presence of amorphous SnO2 shell, demonstrating the existence of electronic interaction between Cu core and amorphous SnO2 shell. For CuSn NWs/CAir, there are two main peaks located at 953.1 eV and 933.1 eV, corresponding to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 of Cu 2+
. Compared with Cu NWs/C, only a slight positive shift for Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 of CuSn
NWs/C-H2 can be found. The CuSn NWs/C-N2 shows significant changes with higher BEs of 952.4 eV and 932.6 eV for Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2, respectively. To further determine the Cu species, Auger Cu LMM spectra were performed (Figure S18). It is clearly shown that Cu LMM peaks are located about 568.0 eV, which can be assigned to Cu 0 , except that a peak appears at 568.7 eV of Cu 2+ for CuSn NWs/C-Air. Meanwhile, the Sn 3d peaks of various catalysts were also analyzed (Figure 4b). Compared with CuSn NW/C, the peaks of Sn 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 of CuSn NWs/C-air shift to lower BEs of 495.0 eV and 486.5 eV, demonstrating the enhanced electron transfer from Cu to Sn after post-annealing under air. The Sn 4+
peaks of CuSn NWs/C-H2 are similar to that of CuSn NW/C, while two distinct
negative shift peaks with BEs of 494.9 eV and 486.4 eV can be seen for CuSn NWs/C-N2. The chemical states and electronic properties changes of different catalysts clearly show that the electronic interaction between Cu and Sn species have been readily modulated by controlling thermal annealing in different atmospheres. The modulated chemical and electronic properties will further tune the binding strength of CO2RR intermediates (described by the d-band center), eventually determining the selectivity for final products. We can see that, compared with Cu NWs/C the d-band center of different CuSn NWs/C shifts towards Fermi level after introducing the Sn species (Figure 4c), demonstrating the stronger binding
strength to HCOO* intermediate.[34,35] Although d-band center of CuSn NWs/C-H2 is the closest to the Fermi level, the competitive adsorption of hydrogen on the surface of CuSn NWs/C-H2 is superior to those of CuSn NWs/C and CuSn NWs/C-Air, resulting in decreased HCOOH selectivity, which is also confirmed by the following theoretical calculation.
We also implemented first-principles calculations to investigate the origin of CO2RR enhancement
in CuSn NWs/C-Air. According to the aforementioned morphology and structure analysis, we constructed different surface models to represent the potential reaction sites for CuSn NWs after thermal annealing in different atmospheres (Figure 5a). The CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2 could be simplified into Sn atoms doping CuO(111), SnO2(110) surface loaded by a Cu4 cluster and pristine SnO2(110) surface models, respectively. The electrocatalytic CO2RR and HER pathways were then compared based on the Gibbs free energy change. Considering the best performance of HCOOH product in various catalysts at -1.0 V vs. RHE, the computational applied electrode potential was set to -1.0 V vs. RHE accordingly. The free energy diagrams of CO2RR show that the HCOOH product pathways were energetically favorable on the surfaces of Sn atoms doping CuO(111), SnO2(110) surface loaded by a Cu4 cluster models than pristine SnO2(110) model due to the spontaneous energy decrease after CO2 molecule combined with a pair of electron and proton into *OCHO (Figure 5b). However, we found that free energy along HER pathway could become more negative than that of CO2RR on CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, which means that they could also facilitate H2 production because the Gibbs adsorption free energy of hydrogen atom (0.14 eV) was more close to zero (Figure 5c). Thus, CuSn NWs/C-Air could not only facilitate HCOOH production but also suppress hydrogen adsorption, resulting in high selectivity of HCOOH in the experiments.
Fig 5. (a) Optimized surface models for CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2, in which red, green and gray balls represent the oxygen, copper and tin atoms. Gibbs free energy change of (b) CO2RR and (c) HER on different surfaces under the applied electrode potential of -1.0 V vs. RHE.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we have successfully created a new class of CuSn NWs with controlled phases and structures as superior electrocatalysts for CO2RR. By the combination of efficient hydrothermal process and facile post-annealing treatment, three distinct CuSn NWs/C-Air, CuSn NWs/C-H2 and CuSn NWs/C-N2 have been successfully created. Significantly, the optimized CuSn NWs/C-Air with modulated phase and structure exhibits the best CO2RR activity with FEHCOOH up to 90.2% at -1.0 V vs. RHE under 0.5 M KHCO3, which is much higher than those of CuSn NWs/C-H2 (62.6%) with heterostructure and CuSn NWs/C-N2 (64.3%) with core-shell structure. The CuSn NWs/C-Air also shows outstanding durability with stable HCOOH product after continuous electrocatalysis for 10 h. The high HCOOH selectivity of CuSn NWs/C-Air is mainly attributed to the Sn atoms on the CuO(111)
surface, which could enhance the adsorption of CO2 intermediate * OCHO and suppress H2 production. We infer that the hierarchical NWs with controlled phases and structures can provide high potential for designing high-performance CO2RR electrocatalysts and beyond.

sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text:
For the first time, a series of bimetallic CuSn NWs with modulated phases and
structures as superior electrocatalysts for CO2RR have been developed.
 The optimized CuSn NWs/C-Air exhibits the boosted electrochemical CO2RR
activity with FEHCOOH of 90.2% at -1.0 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (vs. RHE), and also enhanced durability with negligible degradation after operation for up to 10 h.
 Density functional theory calculations reveal that Sn atoms doping into CuO(111)
surface, enhancing the adsorption of CO2 intermediate * OCHO and suppressing H2 production, could be the plausible site to realize the high selective CO2RR observed in CuSn NWs/C-Air.
